claims.claim: Let D(m,n) be the maximum push number of a sortable m×n instance, N=mn, s=min{m,n}, and t=max{m,n}. Then D(m,n)=O(N·min{s,log t}).
claims.evidence: Assume the source's standing regime 2≤m≤n. For a p×q board, the FillColumns proof does not require p≤q: each column rotates at most p−1 times. If f columns are underfull, then q buffer-row rotations lower the wrong-body potential by at least f/2. In a phase q/2^i≤f<q/2^(i−1), the potential is at most (p−1)q/2^(i−1), allowing fewer than 4(p−1) full q-rotation blocks, hence O(pq log q) total pushes. Applying this with (p,q)=(n,m) to the transpose, then FloatMinimums, establishes correct original-row membership in O(N log m). An even permutation of any selected row is the product of two involutions with equal transposition counts; the corresponding opposite-direction SwapPairs operations use identical auxiliary columns, so their body shifts cancel and the cost is O(N). Odd row permutations are handled by one row rotation when n is even, by correcting the even body cycle of length m−1 when n is odd and m is even, and, when both are odd, by pairing the necessarily even number of odd row permutations. For adjacent rows, (a b c)(a d c)=(a b)(c d) in the source's left-to-right convention, and each L-cycle is an exact four-push commutator. Telescoping these gadgets pairs arbitrary rows in O(m) pushes per pair, totaling O(m²)≤O(N). Sorting m rows therefore costs O(mN). Combining O(Nm) with the source's O(N log n) bound and transposition symmetry proves O(N·min{s,log t}). The local identities were also checked exactly for all dimensions 2 through 8.
claims.search_method: Independent potential analysis, positional-permutation proof for every parity case, and exact enumeration of the commutator and telescoping identities.

claims.claim: For every fixed s≥2, boards with min{m,n}=s have asymptotically tight push number D(m,n)=Θ(mn).
claims.evidence: Claim 0 gives D(s,t)=O(st·s)=O(st) for each fixed s. Translating the sorted board by floor(t/2) columns and floor(s/2) rows has exact distance s·floor(t/2)+t·floor(s/2), which is Ω(st) for every fixed s≥2. Thus D(s,t)=Θ(st) as t grows.
claims.witness: For each fixed s≥2, use the sorted s×t board translated by floor(t/2) columns and floor(s/2) rows.
claims.search_method: Combined the independently proved O(Ns) construction with the displacement lower-bound family; exact small-board translation distances were cross-checked by BFS.

claims.claim: Every instance A has the displacement certificate pn(A)≥ceil(H(A)/n)+ceil(V(A)/m). Moreover, a global translation by a columns and b rows has exact push number m·d_n(a)+n·d_m(b), where d_k(z)=min(z mod k,k−(z mod k)).
claims.evidence: Cyclic graph distance is 1-Lipschitz across a unit edge. Consequently, a row push changes H by at most n and no column push changes H, so at least ceil(H/n) row pushes are required. Symmetrically, at least ceil(V/m) column pushes are required; these disjoint move counts add. For a global translation, every one of the mn tokens has horizontal distance d_n(a) and vertical distance d_m(b), giving lower bound m·d_n(a)+n·d_m(b). Rotating every row in a shortest reverse direction d_n(a) times and every column d_m(b) times attains that bound. For an unsortable instance, the inequality is immediate under the standard pn=∞ convention; the source otherwise uses pn on sortable instances. Exact BFS checked the certificate for every reachable state of 2×2, 2×3, 2×4, and 3×3 boards—222,504 states total—and checked every global translation on those boards.
claims.witness: The global translation itself attains equality: independently reverse all row and column translations along shortest cyclic directions.
claims.search_method: Analytic Lipschitz-potential proof plus exhaustive exact-state BFS checks on four complete Cayley graphs.

claims.claim: A sharper general counting lower bound is D(m,n)≥ceil(log_{d−1}(1+(d−2)(Q−1)/d)), where d=2(m+n), Q=(mn)! if m or n is even, and Q=(mn)!/2 otherwise.
claims.evidence: In the source's standing m,n≥2 domain, the parity characterization gives exactly Q sortable configurations. There are d nominal directed generators. A shortest word contains no adjacent generator followed by its inverse, so the number of configurations representable within L pushes is at most 1+d·sum_{j=0}^{L−1}(d−1)^j=1+d((d−1)^L−1)/(d−2). Since all Q sortable configurations lie within the diameter, substituting L=D and rearranging yields the displayed ceiling logarithm. Duplicate transformations in size-two rows or columns only make this word count a looser upper bound. All numerical decisions in the checker used the equivalent integer inequality d((d−1)^L−1)≥(d−2)(Q−1), without floating point. The resulting bounds 2,3,5,5 were below the exact diameters 4,7,10,8 for 2×2, 2×3, 2×4, and 3×3.
claims.search_method: Independent nonbacktracking-word count, algebraic rearrangement, and exact-integer comparison against complete small Cayley graphs.

claims.claim: Global translations are not generally diametral: D(2,3)=7, whereas every translated 2×3 board has distance at most 5.
claims.evidence: Independent exact BFS using the seven distinct 2×3 unit transformations reached all 720 configurations. Its level histogram was [1,7,31,115,274,253,36,3], so the diameter is 7. Applying the stated seven pushes to the identity produces rows (3,2,1) and (6,5,4), whose BFS distance is 7. Enumeration of all six global translations gave distances 0,3,2,5,2,5, hence maximum 5.
claims.witness: Configuration ((3,2,1),(6,5,4)); shortest word R1-left, C1-up, R1-left, C1-up, C3-up, R1-right, C1-up.
claims.search_method: Exhaustive exact breadth-first traversal of the complete 2×3 Cayley graph, followed by exact witness replay and enumeration of every global translation.

target_evidence: The exact target asks for asymptotically tight general bounds closing the remaining multiplicative Θ(log max{m,n}) gap. The draft does not do that: when s≥log t, its surviving general bounds remain Ω(N) versus O(N log t). It does, however, prove material new partial progress—O(Ns), hence O(N·min{s,log t}), and a tight Θ(N) classification for every fixed-width family. The final writeup explicitly acknowledges the unresolved logarithmic general gap, so its claimed resolution of PARTIAL is accurate and its coverage is not overstated.
